core_idea: a place where money is kept safe, or the raised ground beside a river

senses.definition: a business that keeps and lends money and provides other financial services
senses.explanation: You keep your money in an account at a bank, and you can borrow money from a bank. The word is also used for the building where this business is done.

examples.text: Mari opened an account at the bank near her office.
The bank agreed to lend them the money for the house.
Is there a bank open on Sunday?

compare.note: a building society is owned by its members

subsenses.definition: a store of something that is kept ready to be used when it is needed
subsenses.explanation: The thing stored is named before the word: a blood bank, a bank of questions.

examples.text: The hospital keeps a blood bank for emergencies.
Every test is made from a large bank of questions.

senses.definition: the raised ground along each side of a river, a stream, or a lake
senses.explanation: A river has two banks. You stand or sit on the bank, and a river that floods bursts its banks.

examples.text: Sam sat on the bank and watched the boats go by.
After the heavy rain, the river burst its banks.
Tall grass grew along the banks of the stream.

synonyms.note: shore is used for the sea and for large lakes

adaptation.semantic: Many languages use one word for the side of a river and the side of the sea. In English, bank is used only for rivers, streams, and lakes; the land beside the sea is the shore or the coast.

phrases.definition: to cost more money than a person can afford
phrases.explanation: Usually used in the negative: something that will not break the bank is cheap enough to buy without worrying.

examples.text: A weekend by the sea will not break the bank.
Kim wanted a present that would not break the bank.

adaptation.culture: The phrase comes from gambling: a player who wins more than the house can pay is said to break the bank. Most speakers use it without thinking of games.

word_family.note: to put money in a bank

synonym_discrimination.note: A bank is the ground beside a river, a stream, or a lake. The shore is the land beside the sea or a large lake. The coast is the whole stretch of land next to the sea, seen on a map.

usage_note: When you talk about your own money, say that it is in the bank, not at the bank: My savings are in the bank. You go to the bank to put money in or take it out.

learner_errors.note: Bank is a countable noun and needs a determiner such as the or a.

etymology.text: The money sense came into English from Italian banca, a bench or counter where a money changer did business. The river sense is older and comes from a Germanic word for a ridge or slope. The two were later felt to be one word.

adaptation.semantic: English uses one word for the money bank and the river bank, which are separate words in most languages. The two meanings are unrelated in origin, so it helps to learn them as two words that happen to be spelled the same.
adaptation.grammar: Bank is countable: a bank, two banks. Learners often leave out the article and say go to bank instead of go to the bank.
adaptation.culture: In English-speaking countries a bank is also where people get cash, pay bills, and change money, so the word comes up often in everyday talk about shopping and travel.
adaptation.false_friends: In several languages a word that looks like bank means a bench or a seat. In English, bank never means a seat.
adaptation.pronunciation: The vowel is the short a of cat. The n is pronounced like the ng of sing because it comes before k, so the word rhymes with thank.
